claims.text: The initial material is a multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy with an interpenetrating solid-solution and secondary intermetallic or Laves-phase microstructure.
The alloy initially has a continuous protective oxide or passive surface layer at room and moderately elevated temperatures.
Mechanical wear at elevated temperature disrupts the protective passive layer.
Wear-induced film disruption exposes heterogeneous phase boundaries.
Electrochemical-potential differences between exposed phases create galvanically active microregions and localized corrosion.
Elevated temperature accelerates ionic transport and reaction kinetics, thereby intensifying corrosion.
Localized corrosion weakens microstructural cohesion and increases susceptibility to wear.
Wear-assisted corrosion and corrosion-assisted wear form a mutually reinforcing degradation loop.
Total degradation during simultaneous wear and corrosion will be significantly greater than the sum of degradation in isolated wear-only and corrosion-only tests.
The wear rate under simultaneous exposure will exceed the wear rate in the matched wear-only baseline.
The corrosion rate under simultaneous exposure will exceed the corrosion rate in the matched corrosion-only baseline.
The proposed behavior is expected above approximately 900 °C but below the alloy melting temperature.
The mechanism requires temperatures that enhance diffusion and reaction kinetics without entirely changing phase stability.
The mechanism requires a multiphase eutectic microstructure with distinct phase boundaries capable of galvanic interaction.
A controlled comparison should include wear-only, corrosion-only, and simultaneous wear-corrosion groups tested for matched durations and under matched applicable conditions.
Mass loss, profilometry, microscopy, and electrochemical measurements can be used to distinguish additive from synergistic degradation.
Failure of simultaneous exposure to produce degradation significantly greater than the additive isolated-exposure result would falsify the proposed synergistic-coupling hypothesis.
The magnitude of synergy may depend on microstructural scale, phase distribution, phase coupling, oxide stability, and mechanical load.

contradictions.description: The baseline calls for a wear-only specimen under identical environmental conditions, while the simultaneous test uses a corrosive medium. If the wear-only specimen is exposed to that same corrosive medium, it is not genuinely wear-only; if it is not, the environmental conditions are not identical. The intended control conditions therefore need clarification.
